Good morning. Good morning, Chair Randall and members of the board. I want to acknowledge Law's board members, staff, volunteers, community partners, and survivors who are with us in the room and online today. I am Samantha Clark, the CEO of Law's Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault Services. Loudoun County has long been a leader in supporting survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault. For 40 years, laws has been at the forefront, providing trauma-informed survivor services. Our success in Loudoun is rooted in strong partnerships between the county, law enforcement, courts, schools, and many other community-based organizations.

This coordinated approach works. Last year alone, laws provided 91 adults and 88 children, 3,100 nights of emergency shelter. Through advocacy services, 743 survivors received more than 4,000 hours of assistance, and 1,183 hotline calls were answered. We prioritized safety and well-being of children, providing 307 hours of trauma therapy, 144 forensic interviews for child victims, and violence prevention education for more than 1,600 youth and youth-serving professionals. These numbers reflect services expertly delivered and lives saved, families

stabilized, and cycles of violence disrupted. Survivors in Loudoun County know where to turn for trusted services and resources and help because of a system that has been carefully built over four decades between laws, community organizations, and the county to prioritize safety and healing. The shared goal of laws and the county has always been to ensure that survivors receive care without barriers, delays, or fragmentation. As the county considers funding proposed to develop county-led survivor services and coordination, I ask you to consider the

enormous opportunity to build upon the strong foundation we've forged together. As the CEO of laws, I want you to know we are capable and ready to leverage years of collective experience and institutional knowledge to shape a well-coordinated survivor-centered approach with you. Laws is equally and fully committed to standing with the county to help ensure that any new initiatives enhance and reinforce this existing network of care. Loudoun survivors' response is strongest when services are aligned and survivor access is seamless.

Laws is eager to work alongside Loudoun County and our invaluable community partners. Together, we can ensure Loudoun County remains a leader in compassionate, effective survivor services, setting a standard for communities across the Commonwealth. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, and thank you to everyone in Laws who've done such important work.

My name is Becky Hoey, and I'm the Legal Services Director for Laws and our family law attorney. And I'm honored to speak today about the depth of support and continuing services that survivors receive through laws.

Support that extends far beyond crisis intervention and emergency shelter. Too often, when people think about domestic and sexual violence services, they think only of the moment of crisis, the emergency call, the immediate need for safety, the urgent response. And while that moment is critical, true survivor support goes far beyond the immediate response.

Healing, rebuilding, and regaining stability take time. Laws walks alongside survivors for years, providing a continuum of services and skilled support that meet needs at every stage of the journey. Beyond shelter, survivors may need legal advocacy to navigate protective orders, custody issues, divorce matters.

Some may need trauma-informed, survivor-focused therapy to heal from years of abuse. Many need skilled survivor housing advocacy to regain stability. Leaving an abusive situation is not a one-time event, but a nuanced process that requires ongoing support, which Laws has been doing for four decades.

We don't just provide services. We provide skilled, survivor-centered expertise in a wide range of areas. Our team is trained in the complexities of IPV trauma, legal advocacy and representation, mental health and housing. In my role as the family law attorney at Laws for seven years, I've seen how Laws services have helped thousands of survivors rebuild their lives beyond the moment of crisis.

This is the work that we do every day, not just in moments of crisis, but in the months and the years that follow. Laws is eager to work collaboratively with the county to ensure survivors receive highly skilled, survivor-focused, coordinated support across the full continuum of services.

As the county considers funding enhanced services, I ask you to consider aligning your efforts and leveraging laws' unique expertise in providing long-term support so that together we can build a future in Loudoun County where every survivor is supported in both crisis and every step of their journey towards healing.

Together, we can ensure Loudoun County remains a leader in compassionate, effective survivor services, setting a standard for communities across the Commonwealth. thank you. Thank you. Brianna Carr followed by Diana Rodriguez followed by Mildred Perez.

Fear of deportation, language access challenges, distrust of government systems, and concerns about eligibility and confidentiality often prevent them from reaching out for the support they desperately need.

For these survivors, the difference between a community-based service and a government agency is not just a preference. It is a difference between, it is often just a matter of safety. They need resources they can trust.
